sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Lepiota castanea is a small dapperling: its cap is usually 1–4 cm wide, bell-shaped at first, then expanded with a raised centre. The pale cream background is marked with reddish-chestnut scales, densest toward the centre. The gills are whitish to cream and free. The slender stem is pale near the top, reddish brown and finely scaly below; its thin ring is fugitive.

sections.title: Flesh, habitat and spores
sections.text: The whitish flesh may become slightly reddish. The stem is hollow at maturity. The spore print is white; the smooth, spindle-shaped spores have a small lateral spur and are microscopic. The species grows on forest litter and humus in coniferous and broad-leaved woods, alone or in small groups, mainly in summer and autumn.

sections.title: Taxonomy
sections.text: The accepted name is Lepiota castanea Quél. (1881). Small dapperlings with brown or reddish pigments can be difficult to identify without careful examination. A scaly cap or visible ring alone does not establish the species.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: Do not eat: the species is treated as potentially deadly. The presence of amatoxins in Lepiota castanea remains uncertain; some analysed specimens did not contain them. This does not establish that all populations are harmless. If ingestion is suspected, seek urgent medical or poison-centre advice.
